title: Verification and supervision in reasoning tasks
markdown:
## 1 Correct answers can conceal invalid reasoning and reverse model rankings Final-answer checking is sufficient only when the answer is the entire deliverable. For tasks that also require a derivation or a specified execution process, I examine domain assumptions, method applicability, supporting evidence, tool compliance, intermediate results, and the conclusion. The model's displayed CoT and visible reasoning traces are observable outputs that I cross-check against execution records; they are not direct records of its internal reasoning. In the OlympiadBench and Omni-MATH samples later analyzed for *ProcessBench*, 32.2% and 51.8% of solutions with correct final answers still contained process errors (*[ProcessBench, Section 3.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06559v2)*). Answer accuracy and the validity of a reasoning trace are distinct evaluation targets. Suppose problems and model trajectories are drawn from a target capability distribution. Let $`Z = 1`$ indicate that the complete solution, including its reasoning steps and tool execution, is valid, and let $`V = 1`$ indicate that the evaluation protocol accepts it. For model $`m`$, define its true validity rate as $`\theta_m = \Pr_m(Z = 1)`$, its false acceptance rate as $`\alpha_m = \Pr_m(V = 1 \mid Z = 0)`$, and its false rejection rate as $`\beta_m = \Pr_m(V = 0 \mid Z = 1)`$. False acceptance can admit an unsupported derivation or a tool call that produces the correct answer while violating a predefined execution requirement. False rejection can exclude a valid alternative derivation. By the law of total probability: $$ (1) \qquad s_m = E_m[V] = \alpha_m + (1 - \alpha_m - \beta_m)\theta_m, \qquad s_m - \theta_m = \alpha_m(1 - \theta_m) - \beta_m\theta_m $$ The term $`\alpha_m(1 - \theta_m)`$ credits invalid trajectories, while $`-\beta_m\theta_m`$ penalizes valid ones. Adding benchmark problems reduces the sampling variance of $`\hat{s}_m`$ but does not remove the structural gap $`s_m - \theta_m`$. Models can differ in their adherence to evidence requirements, verification steps, and tool permissions. The resulting differences in $`\alpha_m`$ and $`\beta_m`$ can reverse their ranking: • Suppose Models A and B have true validity rates of $`\theta_A = 72\%`$ and $`\theta_B = 64\%`$. • If invalid trajectories pass the final-answer check with probabilities $`\alpha_A = 4\%`$ and $`\alpha_B = 36\%`$, with $`\beta_A = \beta_B = 0\%`$, their observed scores are $`s_A = 73.12\%`$ and $`s_B = 76.96\%`$. The model with the lower rate of fully valid solutions ranks higher. Process supervision extends evaluation to intermediate steps (*[Let's Verify Step by Step, Sections 2 and 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.20050v1)*). I apply this approach to general post-training evaluation by accounting for omissions in reference solutions, accepting valid alternative methods, and enforcing evidence and execution requirements defined before responses are generated. Structural simplification can explain a method or reveal redundant work. A slower solution or a larger number of attempts, however, does not by itself make the solution incorrect. A resource-related rejection requires a hard limit specified in advance. ## 2 Proof obligations organize layered review and allow alternative solutions A task specification defines the domain assumptions and execution constraints $`\Gamma_q`$, the target conclusion $`C_q`$, and the proof obligations needed to establish it. Here, a model trajectory $`\tau`$ consists of visible reasoning and observable execution records. It may use different intermediate lemmas, representations, or orders of deduction. Review concerns the submitted material and whether it fulfills the task's obligations. A directed acyclic dependency graph (DAG) $`G`$ organizes the local soundness check for each node $`v_j`$, together with a global tool-compliance predicate $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{comp}}(\tau) \in \{0, 1\}`$: $$ (2) \qquad \Gamma_q \cup \{v_k : k \in \operatorname{pa}(j)\} \vdash v_j, \qquad \Gamma_q \cup \{v_j : j \in \operatorname{sink}(G)\} \vdash C_q, \qquad \mathcal{T}_{\text{comp}}(\tau) = 1 $$ The symbol $`\vdash`$ denotes valid derivability within a sound domain inference system. The condition $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{comp}}(\tau) = 1`$ certifies that each external tool invocation $`t \in \tau`$ belongs to the task's permitted execution environment $`\mathcal{A}_q`$. If root nodes follow from verified assumptions $`\Gamma_q`$, every dependency is sound, and $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{comp}}(\tau) = 1`$, structural induction over a topological ordering of $`G`$ establishes the full conclusion. This formal argument requires the local derivations to have been verified in a sound system. In production, I divided verification into three layers: 1. Code and rule checks cover directly verifiable parts of an answer, required deliverables, and predefined restrictions on tools, execution environments, and resources. Tool compliance requires $`\mathcal{T}_{\text{comp}}(\tau) = 1`$. A call that violates an explicit hard requirement causes rejection ($`V = 0`$), even when the final answer is correct. 2. LLM-as-a-Judge assists with semantic screening. It flags insufficient evidence, misapplied rules, conclusions that exceed their premises, and gaps in reasoning, linking each concern to the relevant trace, tool response, or intermediate output. These flags help direct further review. 3. Scholars with relevant expertise review questions that require domain judgment, admit several reasonable interpretations, or remain disputed after the first two checks. They examine the evidence, applicability of the method, and conclusion. Questions that cannot be resolved from the available evidence remain open. All three layers use the same observable material. I cross-check the model's displayed CoT and visible reasoning against actual tool calls, intermediate outputs, elapsed time, and attempt counts. For each attempt, I look for new evidence, revised premises, or a change in the state of the solution. This identifies repeated calls, continued use of failed assumptions, and loops that make no progress. Conclusions remain unverified when the necessary execution records are missing. I record efficiency separately from correctness and compliance. Long runtimes, repeated attempts, or exhaustive methods can warrant efficiency analysis; they affect acceptance only when they violate a predefined hard limit. Method applicability also needs its own check. Pointwise convergence at a fixed parameter value does not establish that an approximation remains valid within an optimization, an integral, or an exchange of limits. A claim about the order of accuracy requires an approximation parameter, its domain of validity, and a uniform error bound. When such issues cannot be decided programmatically, an LLM can help locate a concern and a specialist scholar can review the assumptions and derivation. This review carries a different evidentiary status from a checkable formal certificate. For feedback, I record the first failed obligation at node $`v_j`$ and mark its descendant subgraph $`\operatorname{desc}(v_j)`$ as unverified. Locally correct calculations under a false premise do not repair the full derivation. This treatment addresses the ambiguity after an error discussed in *[ProcessBench, Section 3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.06559v2)*. A suspected error awaiting specialist review remains unresolved until that review is complete. ## 3 Error certificates for a programmatically verifiable subfamily To test the programmatic layer, I use an optimization subfamily whose constraints and certificates can be checked explicitly. It tests whether certificate checks reject invalid submissions while retaining valid alternative proofs. Consider the equality-constrained strongly convex quadratic problem: $$ (3) \qquad v^* = \min_{Ax = b} f(x), \qquad f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^\top H x + c^\top x, \qquad H \succeq \mu I, \quad \mu > 0 $$ Here $`H`$ is symmetric, $`Ax = b`$ is feasible, and $`\mu > 0`$ is a verified lower bound on curvature. For any feasible candidate $`x`$ satisfying $`Ax = b`$, choose any dual multiplier vector $`\nu`$ and define the stationarity residual $`r = Hx + c + A^\top \nu`$. Strong convexity gives the first inequality below for every feasible displacement $`d \in \ker A`$. Completing the square in $`d`$ gives an exact optimality error certificate: $$ (4) \qquad f(x + d) \ge f(x) + r^\top d + \frac{\mu}{2}\|d\|^2 $$ $$ \inf_{d \in \ker A} \left( r^\top d + \frac{\mu}{2}\|d\|^2 \right) = -\frac{\|P_{\ker A} r\|_2^2}{2\mu} $$ $$ 0 \le f(x) - v^* \le \frac{\|P_{\ker A} r\|_2^2}{2\mu} $$ The operator $`P_{\ker A}`$ is the orthogonal projection onto the space of feasible directions $`\ker A`$. It removes residual components normal to the constraints, which do not affect optimality along the feasible manifold (*[Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Sections 5.5 and 9.1](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxbook.pdf)*). A zero projected residual, $`P_{\ker A} r = 0`$, certifies exact optimality. Otherwise, the certificate bounds the suboptimality gap in objective units: • Solutions derived through Lagrange multipliers or by eliminating the equality constraints can satisfy the same semantic obligations and pass verification. • Reporting the correct optimal value $`v^*`$ alone does not fulfill these obligations. Feasibility and the claimed objective value must be checked separately. If a submission claims a KKT multiplier witness, its full stationarity equation $`Hx+c+A^\top\nu=0`$ must also be verified. The projected-residual bound cannot validate that multiplier, since $`P_{\ker A}A^\top\nu=0`$ for every $`\nu`$. A valid equality-elimination proof need not supply a multiplier witness. I use the lessons from this subfamily to structure general review: check the inputs and assumptions, compliance with the execution specification, support for the derivation, and whether the conclusion exceeds the evidence. Rules or certificate verifiers handle obligations that admit programmatic checks. Other semantic questions go through LLM-assisted screening and specialist review. Structural simplification may explain why a method needs less repeated work, but efficiency gains and validity certificates are evaluated separately. ## 4 Task transformations must propagate error bounds Symbolic templates parameterize variable domains and answer formulas (*[GSM-Symbolic, Section 3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.05229v1)*). Tasks with formalizable transformations also need verifiable rules for how those transformations affect feasible sets, objective values, and acceptance tolerances. Let an original problem and its transformed variant have feasible sets $`F`$ and $`F'`$, objectives $`J`$ and $`J'`$, and finite infima $`v`$ and $`v'`$. Suppose the task designer verifies a bijection $`\Phi : F \to F'`$ such that every feasible $`u \in F`$ satisfies the uniform bound: $$ (5) \qquad |J'(\Phi(u)) - aJ(u) - b| \le \varepsilon, \quad a > 0 $$ $$ av + b - \varepsilon \le v' \le av + b + \varepsilon $$ $$ J(u) - v \le \delta \implies J'(\Phi(u)) - v' \le a\delta + 2\varepsilon $$ Taking infima in the first line gives the second. Subtracting the lower bound on $`v'`$ from the upper bound on $`J'(\Phi(u))`$ gives the third. The result determines the acceptance tolerance for a previously $`\delta`$-optimal solution after a unit conversion, parameter rescaling, or numerical transformation with error bounded by $`\varepsilon`$. Keeping the original tolerance $`\delta`$ can misclassify a valid transformed solution as a model failure; relaxing it arbitrarily can conceal a real capability gap. When $`\varepsilon = 0`$, the bijection and positive scaling $`a > 0`$ also preserve whether an optimum is attained. Changes to boundary compactness or admissible control classes require a new attainment proof. ## 5 Grading errors change the post-training objective Step-level labels can improve post-training only if they measure logical validity and compliance. Systematic grading errors pass into the targets used by process reward models (PRMs) and RLHF policies. Let $`h`$ denote the task input and the model's visible reasoning prefix through the current step. Let $`Z = 1`$ indicate that the step is valid under the problem's assumptions, and let $`V \in \{0, 1\}`$ be the grader's noisy acceptance label, with conditional false acceptance $`\alpha(h)`$ and false rejection $`\beta(h)`$. Writing $`p(h) = \Pr(Z = 1 \mid h)`$, a process evaluator with logit $`s`$ trained by binary cross-entropy is optimized toward the corrupted conditional target: $$ (6) \qquad \tilde{p}(h) = \alpha(h) + [1 - \alpha(h) - \beta(h)]p(h) $$ $$ \frac{\partial \ell(s, V)}{\partial s} = \sigma(s) - V $$ $$ E[\nabla_s \ell(s, V) - \nabla_s \ell(s, Z) \mid h] = p(h) - \tilde{p}(h) $$ The expected gradient difference describes how grading bias changes the training target: • If false rejection dominates, $`\beta(h)p(h) > \alpha(h)[1-p(h)]`$, then $`\tilde{p}(h) < p(h)`$. The learned validity target shifts downward, penalizing valid alternative proofs. • If false acceptance dominates, $`\alpha(h)[1-p(h)] > \beta(h)p(h)`$, then $`\tilde{p}(h) > p(h)`$. The target shifts upward, rewarding flawed proofs or noncompliant tool calls. The effects cancel in the conditional mean when their weighted contributions are equal. When $`\alpha, \beta`$ are known constants with $`\alpha + \beta < 1`$, class-conditional noise correction can remove bias from the mean estimate (*[Learning with Noisy Labels, Sections 2 and 3](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2013/file/3871bd64012152bfb53fdf04b401193f-Paper.pdf)*). It also increases variance by the following squared factor: $$ (7) \qquad \hat{\theta}_{\text{corr}} = \frac{\bar{V} - \alpha}{1 - \alpha - \beta}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}_{\text{corr}}) = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\bar{V})}{(1 - \alpha - \beta)^2} $$ For task families whose validity is exactly decidable by a sound and complete certificate verifier, $`\alpha=\beta=0`$ removes this variance penalty. The stress test below evaluates the certificate method within such a programmatically decidable subfamily. Error rates for LLM-assisted labels and specialist review require separate calibration samples. ## 6 Reproducible tests of false acceptance and false rejection I constructed 600 strongly convex quadratic task families to test the certificate verifier within this subfamily. Using exact rational arithmetic, I generated 6 algebraic submissions per family, for 3,600 submissions in total: • 1,200 valid certificates, 2 per family: one derived using Lagrange multipliers and one using equality elimination. • 2,400 submissions with controlled defects, 4 per family: (1) an infeasible construction, $`Ax \neq b`$, that yields the exact optimal value $`v^*`$; (2) failure of stationarity along a feasible direction in $`\ker A`$ while reporting $`v^*`$; (3) a claimed multiplier that fails the stationarity equation while reporting $`v^*`$; and (4) an incorrect final objective value. The first three classes, comprising 1,800 submissions or 75% of all invalid submissions, report the correct final answer $`v^*`$. We compared three deterministic acceptance protocols on all 3,600 submissions:
Acceptance protocolFalse acceptance rate on invalid certificates ($`2,400`$)False rejection rate on valid certificates ($`1,200`$)Valid share of accepted submissions
Final-answer matching only75.0% (accepts 1,800 flawed solutions)0.0%40.0%
Strict reference-path matching (ablation)0.0%50.0% (rejects 600 valid elimination proofs)100.0%

Within this exact-arithmetic benchmark, semantic certificate verification accepted 1,800 fewer invalid proofs than final-answer matching and retained 600 more valid alternative solutions than strict reference-path matching. It also passed all 600 feasible-perturbation checks on the projected-residual bound in Equation (4). Here, semantic certificate verification checks the constraints, objective value, and certificate conditions explicitly. The reported error rates apply to this constructed benchmark. LLM-assisted screening and review by specialist scholars are evaluated separately. ## 7 Dependence within task families and the cost of expert review Surface variations of one problem template do not provide independent observations of general reasoning ability. Suppose there are $`F`$ independent task families, each with $`K`$ variants, common marginal variance $`\sigma^2`$, and common pairwise within-family correlation $`\rho`$. The variance of the sample mean and the effective sample size $`n_{\text{eff}}`$ are: $$ (8) \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\bar{Z}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{FK}[1 + (K - 1)\rho], \qquad n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{FK}{1 + (K - 1)\rho} $$ For $`F = 50`$ families with $`K = 8`$ variants each, there are $`400`$ responses. If $`\rho = 0.6`$, those $`400`$ responses provide the same precision as $`n_{\text{eff}} \approx 77`$ independent observations. Training and test sets therefore need to be split by task family. New tasks should vary assumptions, evidentiary relationships, or the structure of a derivation, beyond simply substituting numbers. I account for the cost of certificate verification and human review separately within the programmatically verifiable subfamily. The following model compares automated certificate checking with the original workflow of reviewing every submission. The full three-layer process also incurs costs for model calls, calibration, and review of disputed cases. Let $`C_0`$ be the upfront engineering cost of the proof-obligation certificates and verifier, $`c_e`$ the original expert review cost per submission, $`c_v`$ the automated verifier's unit execution cost, and $`u`$ the fraction of submissions escalated to human adjudication. Once false acceptance and false rejection standards are met, assume unit costs are stable and the same expert unit cost applies to escalated cases. The certificate workflow then reduces total cost when submission volume $`N`$ exceeds: $$ (9) \qquad C_0 + N(c_v + uc_e) < Nc_e \iff N > \frac{C_0}{(1 - u)c_e - c_v}, \qquad (1 - u)c_e > c_v $$ The evaluation workflow combines task specifications, visible reasoning, execution evidence, and layered review, with exact certificates where the problem class permits them. I report correctness, compliance, and efficiency separately, preserving the scope and evidentiary status of each assessment.
